source_text: Sed erroris istius haereticorum inde, ut opinor, nata materia est, quia inter filium dei et filium hominis nihil arbitrantur interesse, ne facta distinctione et homo et deus Iesus Christus facile comprobetur. eundem enim atque ipsum, id est hominem filium hominis etiam filium dei, uolunt uideri, ut homo et caro et fragilis illa substantia eadem atque ipse filius dei esse dicatur; ex quo, dum distinctio filii hominis et filii dei nulla secernitur, sed ipse filius hominis dei filius uindicatur, homo tantummodo Christus idem atque filius dei asseratur. per quod nituntur excludere: uwerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis; et uocabitis nomen eius Emmanuel, quod est interpretatum nobiscum deus. Proponunt enim atque illa praetendunt, quae in euangelio Lucae relata sunt, ex quibus asserere conantur, non quod est, sed tantum illud quod uolunt esse: spiritus sanctus ueniet in te, et uirtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi; propterea et quod ex te nascetur sanctum, uocabitur filius dei. si ergo, inquiunt, angelus dei dicit ad Mariam, quod ex te nascetur sanctum, ex Maria est substantia carnis et corporis. hanc autem substantiam, id est sanctum hoc quod ex illa genitum est, filium dei esse proposuit. homo, inquiunt, ipse, et illa caro corporis, illud quod sanctum est dictum, ipsum est filius dei; ut et cum dicit scriptura sanctum, Christum filium hominis hominem intellegamus, et cum jiium dei proponit, non deum sed hominem percipere debeamus. Sed enim scriptura diuina haereticorum et fraudes et furta facile conuincit et detegit. si enim sic esset tantummodo: spiritus ueniet in te, et uirtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi; propterea quod nascetur ex te sanctum, uocabitur filius dei, fortasse alio esset nobis genere aduersus illos reluctandum, et alia nobis essent argumenta quaerenda et arma sumenda, quibus illorum et insidias et praestigias uinceremus. cum autem ipsa scriptura caelesti abundans plenitudine sese haereticorum istorum calumniis exuat, facile ipso quod scriptum est nitimur, et errores istos sine ulla dubitatione superamus. non enim dixit, ut iam expressimus, propterea quod ex te nascetur sanctum, sed adiecit coniunctionem: ait enim, propterea et quod ex te nascetur sanctum; ut illud ostenderet, non principaliter hoc sanctum, quod ex illa nascitur, id est istam carnis corporisque substantiam, filium dei esse, sed consequenter et in secundo loco: principaliter autem filium dei esse uerbum dei incarnatum per illum spiritum, de quo angelus refert: sf7zvitus ueniet in te, et uirtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Hic est enim legitimus dei filius, qui ex ipso deo est, qui dum Sanctum istud assumit et sibi filium hominis annectit et illum ad se rapit atque transducit, conexione sua et permixtione sociata praestat, et filium illum dei facit, quod ille naturaliter non fuit; ut principalitas nominis istius fs dei in spiritu sit domini, qui descendit et uenit; ut sequella nominis in filio dei et hominis sit, et merito consequenter hic filius dei factus sit, dum non principaliter filius dei est. atque ideo dispositionem istam angelus uidens et ordinem istum sacramenti expediens, non sic cuncta confundens ut nullum uestigium distinctionis collocarit, distinctionem posuit, dicendo: propterea et quod nascetur ex te sanctum, uocabitur filius dei: ne si distributionem istam cum libramentis suis non dispensasset, sed in confuso permixtam reliquisset, uere occasionem haereticis contulisset, ut hominis filium, qua homo est, eundem et dei et hominis filium pronuntiare deberent. nunc autem partiticulatim exponens, tam magni sacramenti ordinem atque rationem euidenter expressit, ut diceret, e quod ex te nascetur sanctum, uocabitur filius dei, probans quoniam filius dei descendit: qui dum filium hominis in se suscepit, consequenter illum filium dei fecit; quoniam illum filius sibi dei sociauit et iunxit, ut dum filius hominis adhaeret in natiuitate filio dei, ipsa permixtione feneratum et mutuatum teneret, quod ex natura propria possidere non posset. ac sic facta est angeli uoce, quod nolunt haeretici, inter filium dei hominisque, cum sua tamen sociatione, distinctio, urgendo illos uti Christum, hominis filium hominem, intellegant quoque dei filium, et hominem dei filium, id est dei uerbum (sicut scriptum est) deum, accipiant, atque ideo Christum Iesum dominum (ut ita dixerim) ex utroque contextum atque concretum, et in eadem utriusque substantiae concordia mutui ad inuicem foederis confibulatione sociatum, hominem et deum, scripturae hoc ipsum dicentis ueritate, cognoscant.
pass_a_gloss: But the matter of this error of heretics, as I think, is born from this, that they consider there to be no difference between the Son of God and the son of man, so that, with a distinction made, both the man and God, Jesus Christ, may be easily proven. For they want the same one, that is, the son of man, also to be the Son of God, so that the man and the flesh and that fragile substance may be said to be the same as the Son of God; from which, while the distinction between the son of man and the Son of God is not separated, but the son of man is defended as the Son of God, Christ is asserted to be only a man and the same as the Son of God. Through which they strive to exclude: the Word was made flesh and dwelled in us; and you will call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted as God with us. For they propose and allege those things that are related in the Gospel of Luke, from which they try to assert, not what is, but only what they want to be: the Holy Spirit will come into you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore, what will be born from you will be called holy, and will be called the Son of God. If, therefore, the angel of God says to Mary that what will be born from her will be holy, they say that the substance of flesh and body is from Mary. And this substance, that is, this holy thing born from her, they propose to be the Son of God. The man himself, they say, and that flesh of the body, which is called holy, is the Son of God; so that when the Scripture says holy, we should understand Christ, the son of man, to be a man, and when it proposes the Son of God, we should perceive not God, but a man. But divine Scripture easily convicts and reveals the frauds and thefts of heretics. For if it were only so: the Spirit will come into you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore, what will be born from you will be called the Son of God, perhaps we would have another kind of argument against them, and we would have to seek other arguments and take up other arms, with which we would overcome their snares and deceptions. But since the Scripture itself, abundant with heavenly fullness, strips itself of the calumnies of these heretics, we easily rely on what is written, and we overcome these errors without any doubt. For it did not say, as we have already expressed, therefore what will be born from you will be holy, but it added a conjunction: for it says, therefore and what will be born from you will be holy; so that it might show that this holy thing, which is born from her, that is, this substance of flesh and body, is not primarily the Son of God, but secondarily: but primarily the Son of God is the Word of God incarnate through that Spirit, of which the angel speaks: the Spirit will come into you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. This is indeed the true Son of God, who is from God, who, when he assumes this holy thing and joins the son of man to himself and draws him to himself and leads him across, grants and makes the son of man the Son of God, which he was not naturally; so that the primacy of this name of God is in the Spirit of the Lord, who descends and comes; and the sequence of the name is in the Son of God and man, and deservedly this Son of God is made, since he is not primarily the Son of God. And therefore, the angel, seeing this disposition and expediting the order of this sacrament, did not confuse all things so that no trace of distinction would be placed, but he made a distinction, saying: therefore and what will be born from you will be holy, will be called the Son of God; lest, if he had not dispensed this distribution with its own measures, but had left it confused and mixed, he would have truly given an occasion to heretics, so that they would have to pronounce the son of man, insofar as he is a man, to be the same as the Son of God. But now, expounding particulary, he clearly expressed the order and reason of so great a sacrament, so that he said, what will be born from you will be holy, will be called the Son of God, proving that the Son of God descends: who, when he received the son of man into himself, made him consequently the Son of God; since he associated and joined the son of man to himself, so that when the son of man adheres to the Son of God in birth, he might hold, by this mixture, what he could not possess by his own nature. And so, by the voice of the angel, a distinction is made, which heretics do not want, between the Son of God and the son of man, with their own association, urging them to understand that Christ, the son of man, is a man, and also that he is the Son of God, and that the man is the Son of God, that is, the Word of God, as it is written, God; and therefore they should recognize Christ Jesus, the Lord, as it were, woven and compacted from both, and in the concord of the substance of both, mutually associated by the confibulation of a reciprocal covenant, man and God, the Scripture saying this very thing with truth.

pass_b_english: I believe the source of this heretical error is their refusal to acknowledge any difference between the Son of God and the son of man; otherwise, with a distinction drawn, both the man and God would be easily proven in Jesus Christ. They want the son of man to be identical with the Son of God, so that the man, the flesh, and that fragile substance may be declared to be the very Son of God. Because no distinction separates the son of man from the Son of God, but the son of man is claimed as God's Son, they assert that Christ is only a man and the same as the Son of God. By this they strive to exclude the truth that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and that his name shall be called Emmanuel, which means God with us (Matt. 1:23).

They put forward and allege the words recorded in Luke's Gospel, twisting them to assert not what is true but only what they wish: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). They argue: if the angel tells Mary that what is born from her will be holy, then the substance of flesh and body comes from Mary; and this substance—that holy thing born of her—they claim is the Son of God. The man himself, they say, and that flesh of the body called holy, is the Son of God; so that whenever Scripture says "holy," we must understand Christ the son of man as a mere man, and whenever it presents the Son of God, we must perceive not God but a man.

But divine Scripture easily convicts and exposes the heretics' frauds and thefts. If the angel's words were only "the Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called the Son of God," we might need a different line of argument and other weapons to defeat their snares and deceptions. But Scripture, abounding in heavenly fullness, strips itself of their calumnies; we simply stand on what is written and overcome these errors without doubt. For the angel did not say, as we have shown, merely "therefore the child to be born will be holy"; he added a conjunction: "therefore *and* the child to be born will be holy called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). This shows that the holy thing born of her—this substance of flesh and body—is not primarily the Son of God, but secondarily; primarily the Son of God is the Word of God incarnate through that Spirit of whom the angel speaks: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35).

This is the true Son of God, who is from God. When he assumes this holy thing and joins the son of man to himself, drawing him to himself and leading him across, he grants and makes the son of man the Son of God—which he was not by nature—by the union and mixture joined to himself. Thus the primacy of the divine name rests in the Spirit of the Lord who descends and comes; the sequence of the name belongs to the Son of God and man, and this one rightly becomes the Son of God because he is not primarily the Son of God. Therefore the angel, perceiving this arrangement and expediting the order of this mystery, did not confuse everything so as to leave no trace of distinction; he established a distinction, saying: "therefore and the child to be born will be holy, and will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). Had he not dispensed this distribution with its proper measures but left it confused and mixed, he would have given heretics grounds to pronounce the son of man, as man, to be the same as the Son of God.

Now, expounding particularly, he clearly expressed the order and reason of so great a mystery, saying that the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God, proving that the Son of God descends: who, when he received the son of man into himself, consequently made him the Son of God, because he associated and joined the son of man to himself, so that when the son of man adheres to the Son of God in birth, he might hold by this mixture what he could not possess by his own nature. Thus the angel's voice makes a distinction—which heretics reject—between the Son of God and the son of man, yet with their association, urging them to understand that Christ the son of man is a man, and also to recognize the Son of God, and that the man is the Son of God, that is, the Word of God, who (as Scripture says) is God. Therefore they should know Christ Jesus the Lord as woven and compacted from both, in the concord of both substances, mutually bound by the reciprocal covenant of their union, man and God—Scripture itself declaring this very truth.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of the Latin text regarding the distinction between the Son of God and the son of man. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a polished version that correctly incorporates the necessary scripture citations (Luke 1:35, John 1:14, Matt 1:23) corresponding to the Latin text. The distinction regarding the conjunction 'propterea et quod' is handled correctly in both.
